paragraphs: The benefits that come from attending to private education will always be very limited, and the parent who truly sets his own hand to the plough will always be disappointed to some degree, until education becomes a great national concern. A man cannot withdraw into a wilderness with his child; and even if he did, he could not carry himself back into childhood and become the fitting friend and playmate of an infant or a youth. And when children are restricted to the company of men and women, they very quickly acquire that sort of premature adulthood which halts the growth of every vigorous power of mind or body. To open their faculties, they should be stimulated to think for themselves; and this can be done only by bringing a number of children together and having them pursue the same aims jointly.

A child very soon falls into a numbing laziness of mind, which he seldom has vigour enough to throw off, when he merely asks a question instead of searching for information, and then trusts the answer he is given without question. Among equals in age this could never happen; and the subjects of their inquiry, though they might be influenced, would not be wholly under the direction of men, who often dampen, if they do not destroy, abilities by pushing them forward too quickly. And too quickly they will certainly be pushed forward, if the child could be confined to the company of a man, however shrewd that man may be.

Besides, the seeds of every affection should be sown in youth; and the respectful regard that one feels for a parent is very different from the social affections that are to make up the happiness of life as it goes on. The basis of these is equality, and an exchange of feelings not weighed down by that watchful gravity which discourages argument, even if it does not compel submission. However great a child’s affection for his parent may be, he will always long to play and chatter with other children. And the very respect he feels — for filial esteem always has a touch of fear mixed into it — will, if it does not teach him cunning, at least stop him from pouring out the little secrets that first open the heart to friendship and trust, and lead it by degrees to a wider benevolence. On top of this, he will never acquire that frank openness of behaviour which young people can gain only by being often in company where they dare to say what they think, neither afraid of being rebuked for their presumption nor laughed at for their foolishness.

Struck forcibly by the reflections that the sight of schools, as they are now run, naturally prompted, I once gave my opinion rather warmly in favour of a private education; but further experience has led me to see the subject in a different light. Nevertheless, I still think schools, as they are now regulated, the hotbeds of vice and folly, and I think the knowledge of human nature that is supposed to be gained there is nothing but cunning selfishness.

At school, boys become gluttons and slovens; and instead of developing the domestic affections, they rush very early into the dissipation that ruins the constitution before it is fully formed, hardening the heart as it weakens the understanding.

In fact, I would object to boarding schools if only because of the unsettled state of mind that the expectation of the holidays produces. On these the children’s thoughts are fixed with eager hopes for, to speak moderately, at least half of the time; and when the holidays come, they are spent in utter dissipation and bestial indulgence.

On the other hand, when boys are brought up at home, they may follow a plan of study in a more orderly way than is possible when nearly a quarter of the year is actually spent in idleness, and as much again in regret and anticipation. Yet at home they acquire too high an opinion of their own importance, from being allowed to tyrannize over the servants, and from the anxiety that most mothers show about manners; for these mothers, eager to teach the accomplishments of a gentleman, smother the virtues of a man at birth. So, taken into society when they ought to be seriously occupied, and treated as men while they are still boys, they grow vain and effeminate.

The only way to avoid two extremes that are equally harmful to morality would be to find some means of combining a public and a private education. In this way, to make men citizens, two natural steps might be taken which seem to lead directly to the goal we want. For the domestic affections, which first open the heart to the various forms of human feeling, would be cultivated, while the children would still be allowed to spend a large part of their time with other children on terms of equality.

I still remember with pleasure the country day school, to which a boy trudged in the morning, wet or dry, carrying his books, and his dinner too if it was a good distance away. In those days a servant did not lead the young master by the hand; for once he had put on coat and breeches, he was left to fend for himself and to come home alone in the evening, to tell the exploits of the day at his parents’ knee. His father’s house was his home, and was fondly remembered ever afterwards. Indeed, I appeal to some superior men who were educated in this way: has not the memory of some shady lane where they learned their lesson, or of some stile where they sat making a kite or mending a bat, made their country dear to them?

But what boy ever remembered with pleasure the years he spent in close confinement at an academy near London? Unless, indeed, he happens to recall the poor scarecrow of an assistant master whom he tormented, or the tart-seller from whom he snatched a cake, to devour it with the catlike appetite of selfishness. At boarding schools of every kind, the recreation of the younger boys is mischief, and that of the older boys is vice. Besides, in the great schools, what can be more damaging to moral character than the system of tyranny and abject slavery that is established among the boys, to say nothing of the slavery to forms which makes religion worse than a farce? For what good can be expected from the youth who takes the sacrament of the Lord’s Supper to avoid forfeiting half a guinea, which he will probably spend afterwards on some sensual pleasure? Half the boys’ effort goes into escaping the obligation to attend public worship; and well it may, for such constant repetition of the same thing must be a very tiresome restraint on their natural liveliness. Since these ceremonies have the most fatal effect on their morals, and since a ritual performed by the lips while the heart and mind are far away is no longer stored up by our church as a bank to draw on for the fees of the poor souls in purgatory, why should they not be abolished?

But in this country the fear of innovation extends to everything. It is only a disguised fear, the anxious timidity of lazy slugs who guard, by sliming it over, the snug position that they regard as a hereditary estate, and who eat, drink and enjoy themselves instead of fulfilling the duties, apart from a few empty forms, for which it was endowed. These are the people who insist most strenuously that the founder’s will be observed, crying out against all reform as if it were a violation of justice. I am alluding here especially to the relics of popery retained in our colleges, where the Protestant members seem such sticklers for the established church; yet their zeal never makes them lose sight of the spoils of ignorance which grasping priests of superstitious memory scraped together. No; wise in their generation, they revere the prescriptive right of possession as a stronghold, and still let the sluggish bell tinkle for prayers, as in the days when the elevation of the host was thought to atone for the sins of the people, for fear that one reformation should lead to another, and the spirit kill the letter. These Roman Catholic customs have the most damaging effect on the morals of our clergy. For the idle vermin who, two or three times a day, perform in the most slovenly manner a service they think useless, but call their duty, soon lose all sense of duty. At college, compelled either to attend public worship or to evade it, they acquire a habitual contempt for the very service whose performance is to enable them to live in idleness. It is mumbled through as a matter of business, as a dull boy recites his lesson; and often the college slang slips out of the preacher the moment he has left the pulpit, and even while he is eating the dinner he earned in so dishonest a way.

Nothing, indeed, can be more irreverent than the cathedral service as it is now performed in this country; nor does the country contain a set of weaker men than those who are the slaves of this childish routine. A disgusting skeleton of its former state is still on show; but all the solemnity that engaged the imagination, even if it did not purify the heart, has been stripped away. The performance of high mass on the Continent must impress every mind in which a spark of imagination glows with that awe-filled melancholy, that sublime tenderness, so closely akin to devotion. I do not say that these devotional feelings are of more use, morally speaking, than any other emotion of taste; but I maintain that the theatrical pomp which gratifies our senses is preferable to the cold parade that insults the understanding without reaching the heart.

Among remarks on national education, such observations cannot be out of place, especially as the supporters of these institutions, which have sunk into childishness, pose as the champions of religion. Religion, pure source of comfort in this vale of tears! how your clear stream has been muddied by the dabblers who have presumed to confine in one narrow channel the living waters that flow for ever towards God — the sublime ocean of existence! What would life be without that peace which only the love of God, when built on humanity, can give? Every earthly affection turns back at times to prey upon the heart that feeds it; and the purest outpourings of benevolence, often rudely dampened by men, must rise as a free-will offering to Him who gave them birth, whose bright image they faintly reflect.

In public schools, however, religion, confused with tiresome ceremonies and unreasonable restraints, takes on the most unattractive appearance: not the sober, austere one that commands respect while it inspires fear, but a ridiculous cast that serves as the point of a pun. For in fact most of the good stories and smart sayings that enliven minds which have been concentrating on whist are fashioned out of those very incidents; and the men who labour to give them a comic twist are the very men who countenance the abuse in order to live on its spoils.
